beats.narration_text: Hey, I'm Muskan. Ever notice how an AI's first word takes a moment, but then the rest just streams out? And how a really long chat gets slower and pricier? One idea explains both, and it's quietly doing the heavy lifting in every model you use: the KV cache.

props.command: Why is an AI's first word slow but the rest fast — and why does a long chat cost more?

beats.narration_text: Start with how generation works. A model writes one token at a time. And to pick each new token, it has to look back at every token before it, that's attention. Each past token is stored as two vectors: a Key and a Value. So to generate token number one hundred, the model needs the Keys and Values of all ninety-nine before it.

card.title: How Generation Works.
card.subtitle: one token, looking back at all the rest

items.quote: the model writes token by token
each token attends to all prior ones
each past token = a Key + a Value

card.caption: attention: to choose the next token, the model reads every previous token's Key and Value
card.footer: TOKEN-BY-TOKEN · EACH NEEDS ALL THE PAST

beats.narration_text: Here's the waste, and the fix. Without a cache, every single step recomputes the Keys and Values for the entire history, again and again. Generating a long reply means redoing the same work hundreds of times. The KV cache fixes it: compute each token's Key and Value once, store them, and just reuse them. Every new token now only computes its own.

card.title: Recompute, or Reuse.
card.subtitle: the whole idea
card.caption: cache each token's Key and Value once — never recompute the history
card.footer: RECOMPUTE THE PAST → REUSE THE PAST

beats.narration_text: That's why generation has two phases. First, prefill: the model reads your whole prompt and fills the cache. That's the pause before the first word. Then decode: each new token reuses the cache and only adds itself, which is why the rest streams out fast. Slow start, fast finish, that's the cache being built, then paying off.

card.title: Prefill, Then Decode.
card.subtitle: slow start, fast finish
card.answer: prefill: read the prompt, fill the cache (the pause) → decode: reuse it, stream token by token (fast)
card.caption: the pause before the first word is the cache being built; the fast stream is it paying off

beats.narration_text: But it's not free. The cache has to live in memory, and it grows with every token, times every layer. So for very long contexts, or lots of users at once, it's not compute that runs out first, it's memory. That's the real trade: KV caching spends memory to save compute. Most of the work on long context is really work on shrinking this cache.

show.event: the four trade cards snap in

card.title: Compute for Memory.
card.subtitle: the cache isn't free

items.quote: the cache lives in RAM / VRAM
long context · many users at once

card.caption: for long contexts it's memory, not compute, that runs out first
card.footer: KV CACHING TRADES MEMORY FOR SPEED

beats.narration_text: So, the KV cache: a model generates token by token, and each token needs the Keys and Values of all the ones before it. Cache them once and reuse, instead of recomputing. It's the trade at the heart of fast generation, memory for speed.

artifactLines: Generation is token-by-token, and each new token attends to every previous token — stored as a Key (K) and a Value (V).
Without a cache, every step recomputes all past K/V — the same work, over and over (quadratic).
The KV cache stores each token's K and V once; each new token reuses the past and computes only itself.
The trade: the cache lives in memory and grows with length × layers — for long context, memory is the bottleneck.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Next time you use an AI, watch the timing, the little pause, then the fast stream. That's prefill, then decode. Then ask: if the cache grows with length, what happens to cost and speed as my conversation gets longer? That question is most of what makes long context hard.

props.command: Next time I generate text: watch the pause (prefill, building the cache) then the fast stream (decode, reusing it). If the cache grows with length, what happens to my cost and speed as the chat gets longer?
